blocks.x: Your name, Joe, and I'll have that on here to identify it.
This is Joe Mahrez in New Orleans.
You won't even have to talk towards this. Talk towards me.
Yeah.
This is Bill Russell, so we have to identify who's interviewing. And the date is April the 8th, isn't it?
And where are we, Joe?
We're in the Southland Recording Studios at 520 St. Louis Street here in New Orleans.
Yeah, a lot of famous musicians have recorded a lot in here and played. Those sessions you used to have, I remember, rehearsals and Monday night sessions years ago.
Well, we have probably all the top jazz men that either hit New Orleans from other spots like Chicago and Los Angeles, New York, and so forth. And, of course, all the New Orleans greats.

Someone call. Yeah. To continue, what I wanted to mention on the tape is that you have all of these pictures. It looks like a museum, a wonderful museum of the best collection I've seen of old photos, big and large ones. Let's walk around the room once and tell me something about some of these pictures, the different people.

Well, of course, facing us here, Bill, is the old New Orleans Rhythm Kings. Brother Paul was the leader of that outfit, which I think was the greatest white band to ever sit on a bandstand. That's not only my opinion. That's the opinion of a lot of the greats if you talk to them. And, of course, up here we've got Paul in the middle here.
I might mention that there's a big enlargement about three feet by two and a half or so. And all of these enlargements are around two by three feet or 18 by 14 or something, aren't they?
And that big picture up there is Paul. Paul, that's the Paul, 1920.

I noticed he's holding, not hurry too much, I want to look at that, he's holding a trumpet. What kind of a trumpet did he use? Do you remember anything about him? I don't remember, Bill. I guess it's a trumpet or it could have been a cornet.
It's a trumpet, no. He started out playing cornet, but in that particular picture there he's playing trumpet. It could have been a con, I think, because they were very famous in those days.
They were the most popular here. Yes. Now, on the left here we have a little tailgate himself, Georgie Brunas.
He's puffing his left cheek out. That's right. And on the right here, Paul, we have Leon Rupola, one of the real greats.
Just got a postcard today from someone in Chicago saying that George is opening a new place there now.
Well, George keeps going. He's always the same. In fact, I think he plays the same horn that he played. That is the instrument himself. He still has the same one he played in the early days.
Yeah, we had a nice idea with him last year. Of course, over here to the left is a picture of Sharky, one of New Orleans' real greats that's

left today in the Dixieland field. On the left over here we have Mark Hazel. In my opinion, probably one of the greatest Dixieland drummers in the business. Under him we have Fazola. In my opinion, another one of the real great clarinet players. Him and Rapp, probably the greatest white clarinet players that ever come out of New Orleans.

If there's anything of particular interest about these pictures, if you remember the dates of any of them, like we know the one down below the New Orleans Rhythm Kings, but Paul's, if you remember about the date?

Paul's was taken in 1919 in Chicago. The picture of George is probably 10 years old, probably goes back to 50. I took that picture myself. The picture of Rapp up here goes all the way back to the early 20s, probably 1920.
Does that show much of his clarinet? Can you see much about it? How many keys of it has that?
That was a 13 key.
A 13, that's what I wondered.
Yeah, that's the old Albert system. It's the Albert, of course. And a wooden clarinet. Right above Rapp, we have young Pete Fountain.
You almost read the label, the make on there, the brand, but I guess we can't see it.
That's a very sharp picture.
Really?

Like I said, right above Rapp, we've got Pete Fountain. And Almond Hogg right next to him. Under Almond is Raymond Boyk, another one of the true greats of New Orleans, Dixieland. And to the right of Raymond, we have Santo Pacora, another real great.
Let me interrupt about that picture in your other office. It's the poster, rather. I noticed it was dated up here at the Italian Hall at 1925. Do you know who played that dance?
Yes, that was a benefit for battling Barreau. Paul had Santo and Rapp.
Rapp was still... Oh, Rapp, yeah, Rapp played.

That was in 1925. And they were playing around New Orleans as a unit at that time. But of course, George Brunner stayed in Chicago and Santo Pacora took his place. And we had Leo Addy, one of the real great drummers of that time on drums. And we had Charlie Cadela playing tenor sax. And we had Freddie Newman played piano and Red Long. Both of them played with the outfit. And this particular date, Freddie Newman was playing.
You remember the dance in particular? Oh, yeah. You were there, no doubt.
Yeah, it was at the Italian Hall right here on Esplanade and Rapport, 1925.
It says 75 cents admission. We'll get a copy, a photo, a picture of that some of these days.
Well, that's an old collector's item deal there.
Anything about the dance you can remember, for instance, how they played? They played great.
Oh, yeah. They played all the old numbers like Millen Boyg and Tin Roof Blues and Zero, all those popular numbers.
Did they play many things like ordinary pop tunes, you know, or waltzes or anything? Oh, yeah.

They played the waltzes in Swanee River, old Kentucky home, all that with the beat in it, naturally. Anything that anybody came that thought they'd like to hear, they played it and naturally put the old Rhythm King's beat to it. It was a great band and it done a lot of good for Battlin' Barrella. And the band was really clicking that day because they weren't dancing. They were standing in front of the bandstand. And any time you see that, Bill, that they don't want to dance and listen to the different musicians play, well, then you know that they're playing.
And now let's see if we can go back over here.

Because naturally we've got little Georgie Girard here. He's passed on a few years back. I thought Georgie could have been one of the big names in our music if he'd have lived. But just one of the unfortunate things. But those things happen. Now, above Georgia, we've got old Wingy Minhoom. Everybody knows Wingy. And to the right, Paul Barberin. Everybody knows Paul. King Oliver and Louis Armstrong, drummer. On top, we've got Louis up here holding his trumpet. Of course, I've got Louis in two or three places around the place because, like my favorite, he's everybody else's. And I'm very fond of Louis. Have to be. And different spots here. We've got pictures of old Chink Martin. Old bass boy from, tuba boy from back in the Rhythm King's days. And we've got the late Abby Brunus under Chink Martin. He's drummer. Not the trumpet player, but the drummer. The nephew of Abby Brunus.
This other picture of rap up here. Do you remember where that was taken from? Is that from one of the Rhythm King's?
That's one of the Rhythm Kings and I had blown up, put on this wall right here. That was taken when the band was first organized, the first small band. When we had rap.
That's where he's playing. We could almost count the keys on the clarinet there.

That's right. And that's Jack Pettis in the background there. That's the original first band put together. When Alma Schober was on piano and Jack Pettis on sax and rapping, Paul and Georgie and Mel Stetzel also played a little with the band.
Well, that covers quite a few. I was going to ask, too. At home, you say you have a big collection, too, I imagine. Bill, I have a marvelous collection. I have thousands of them.

This is a fine picture over here that we missed. That's Louie and his Hot Five over there. Johnny St. C. and Johnny Dodds and Louie and Lil Hardin. And actually, over here, we have the Bobcats with Favre and Eddie Miller and with Duke and Nappy Lamar. A lot of New Orleans boys there.
Bill, you asked me about the Southland record.
Well, in my book, New Orleans Jazz Musicians Deserve a Chance to Be Heard. So I decided to see what could be done. The results, I found the Southland Recording Company.
But what date was that?

Well, that was in late 53. I really started out in 54. I thought there was a lot of boys, for instance, like Raymond Boyk, Harry Shields, Ormond Hug, that didn't want to leave New Orleans for different reasons. I thought they should be heard. So I started this little recording company to give the outside people a chance to hear people like Raymond and them. And I think the little label clicked. Up to day, I have probably 17 albums. And so far, the reviewers have been very nice to us. We got some excellent reviewers from all of them, from Downbeat, Jazz Journal. So anybody that listened to the records were very kind to us and very nice. And we appreciate it. And it's helped us. It's helped New Orleans music. It's helped these boys to keep on going. From my little label, fellas like Alvin Alcorn hitched on to Kid Horry. After Kid Horry heard him on my label. Pete Fountain got an awful good break.
Even Al Hurt never recorded before you did, did he?

That's right. I gave Al Hurt his first break on the Southland label. Pete Fountain fronted his first band on my little label. Jack Delaney, Raymond Boyk. Well, there's a lot of fellas that got their first start with Southland. And they went on to bigger and better things with different recording companies. I have all of them, like Johnny Wig, Sharky, Santo Pacora. And most of the top, not most, but all the top boys around New Orleans. My only regret is that I wasn't able to get Paul, my brother. Paul passed on, of course, in 49. And I didn't really start until probably, like I say, in the 50s and went on to 54. 54, yeah.
Mind you, the beginning of your life, the starting, when you were born, where you were raised, what part of town and all? A little bit about your father and your family.
Well, Bill, I was born in 1908, and I come from back on Broad and Espanade. That's back of town in New Orleans.
Can you remember when Paul was born? How much older was he?
Yeah, Paul was born on the turn, at the 1900. Paul would be with the years right now.
He'd be 60 years old. Remember the exact date?
Paul was born in, I think, I don't know the exact date, probably in March somewhere, but I just don't offhand know the date.
What about your father? Did he play any instrument?
My father played trumpet, played good trumpet.
Did he play jazz?

Well, no, he played the Tokyo Gardens out at West End at concerts and stuff. And then my brother Vic, who's two years younger than myself, was a real good tenor man. He took up tenor. In fact, he's got lessons from Skag and Leon. Skag was one of good clarinet players and saxophone men in the late 20s.
Is he the one that played violin too? Did he? No, rap played violin.
Rap started on violin. I don't remember Skag playing violin, but rap originally started on violin.
One thing to interrupt. How do you pronounce your name exactly, and what is it, French or what?
Well, it is French. My daddy was born about maybe 25 miles out of Paris, France.
He was born in France.

He was born in France. Came over and they'd pronounce it different ways. Merez, and if you're in the north, they say Merez. Yeah, how you did for it. Yeah, and Merez, and depends on who's pronouncing it.
But you say...
But we're French people, and my mother's side too is Irish and French. And my sister played piano. My sister played real fine piano. In fact, Paul taught her all the chords and she liked it.
She was younger than you are.

Yeah, she's a year under me. And Vic, getting back to Vic, I thought Vic would have been a real fine tenor man, but he just left it fall on the wayside. I took up clarinet and learned it from rap. I sat next to rap for a year, but I never could learn rap style because, for instance, I used to ask rap, how did you make this lick? How did you make this break? And he used to call me Oibs. And he used to say, well, Oibs, I really can't tell you. I'll make them when I get to them, which was true with rap. Rap never played the same solo back, or he never played the same thing. It was right from the heart, right on the spot.
You can tell that from the Tin Roof Blues. There's three masters. That's right.

They were all different because rap couldn't play the same solos. We have Raymond Boyk in that same category. I could be rehearsing here and tell Raymond would come out with a good solo, and I said, that's the one I want, Raymond. Well, I can't get it back because Raymond's not going to play it anymore the same way. Well, those fellas are really playing from the heart, Bill. Then we came along, and I started out. I went up to Spring Hill College, and that was around the 25, 26. But before that, I had a chance to go to Chicago, and I heard King Oliver and all the greats. Of course, at that time, I didn't appreciate it. I didn't know exactly how great they were until now, you see. And it didn't mean that much to me at that particular time, but I was hearing Baby Dodds and Johnny Dodds and Lee Collins and all the greats, King Oliver and all the Austin High boys and Bix and so forth and all that, but I didn't appreciate it, like I say, because I didn't know what it was all about at the time. That's right. And I would have given my right arm to play clarinet, but for some reason, I just didn't get to be good with it. So Paul told me, look, boy, you either got to be good or it's no good. So I dropped out of it. And, of course, I never lost interest in jazz. I always had it in my heart, and I always went along with it. Wait, I'll catch you somebody else.
You went to Chicago in the early days. Tell me some more about your playing. You probably gave up clarinet.
Well, I used to go sit in with Charlie Cadela and Abby Bernstein at the halfway house and at the Paris Royal later when Abby played there.
Did you ever play professionally or just go around sitting in?

Well, in Biloxi. I played, I wouldn't say professional, but I used to sit in with Julian Lane and all the boys around up there. And, of course, Abby wasn't in Biloxi at that time, but he came over quite a bit and married. And I played with them, but I never really got to be able to play the clarinet like the greats, like Fazola and Rap. And stuff like
those fellas so I just threw it on the west side.
You used the Albert System?

Oh yeah. In fact I still have it. You still have one? I still have the old Albert System clarinet that Rap used when he made She's Crying For Me blues and Golden Leaf Struts. Yes I have it because he used my clarinet. That time he didn't have any. I think he used Harry Shields' mouthpiece. But I had a chance anyhow to hear all the greats and that's one thing I'll always remember. Of course Brother Paul passed on. I think Paul was ready for a comeback and he just passed on and those things happened. Can you tell me
I don't like to bother you with a lot of details but if you can remember everything you can remember about Paul when he started on the coronet was that his first instrument for instance?
No his first thing was trumpet because my daddy played trumpet.
It wasn't anything like piano or guitar or drums.

He didn't play anything else. No but he could play piano. Paul had a good sharp ear and Paul used to play chords and could play piano too and he played just the Tropicos Picnic from my daddy and that's the way he learned it. And around after the World War
Did he start to write the Method book or learn by ear?

No yeah Paul never could read until just a little sight read at the end here and there but then after he went in the Marines and went overseas and Paul came back and around after the war was over 1918 and then from he went up the line on the on the boat.
Is that his first job?
Well he played in New Orleans here all around but that was his first
Do you remember any first band that he played with really?

Well he used to play with rap and Georgie and all they used to all get together in that book town and so forth and he used to sit in like that and go to the halfway house when Abby was there but then Paul went up to Chicago and that's where he stayed and he formed the New Orleans Rhythm Kings. Paul does get credit for putting New Orleans Rhythm Kings together.
Can you remember a little bit of the details of that because we can't talk about it.

Well they tell me what I hear and that Paul of course Paul married a Chicago girl and that particular time he was staying at her mother's home and her brother Tommy Harrison was very friendly with Mike Fritzel and Jacob who owned the Cher Parita Big Night Club in Chicago and owned Fry's Inn before that and Tom told them that New Orleans music was getting to be a big thing around there the original Dixieland had come through and a lot of New Orleans boys Tom Brown and all that came through and they liked the New Orleans music so he asked Mike Fritzel to give Paul a chance to organize a band and Paul sent for Georgie Brunus which he came to my father and my father gave Georgie the train fare to get up there he left with my little brother Rene's little McInerney overcoat and he had his trombone in the newspaper and he went to Chicago that particular time Rap and Santo and Emmett Hardy and those fellas were on the boat line also for B. Palmer
that's what I would ask about her

and there was somewhere in the Indiana port those playing and it wasn't going too good and then Paul sent for rap for rap rap joined the band they had the little Deacon Lloyd Kanner he's on bass and he had Elmer Schober and Frank Snyder on drums that was the voice and small band and later on they took on Mel Stetzel on piano Paul was on trumpet and rap and Georgie was the front line and it took in Steve Brown on bass which was the finest and Lou Black they added on banjo and it took Benny Pollack who was a very very young good drummer and Paul liked him and Paul gave him a chance to come on in
you know anything about Black where he came from I don't know

the New Orleans Rhythm Kings were probably the most popular jazz band in the country Jelly Roll Morton was just floating around and really couldn't get too much work around there and he was plugging tunes for Melrose Brothers Melrose Brothers asked Jelly Roll at least told him to go see Paul Merez you got some nice tunes here and he's from New Orleans and Jelly Roll knew him and Jelly Roll came over to see Paul and told him about the tunes he had and so forth and Paul had a session coming up with Jeanette Records and Jelly Roll played a tune for him called Mr. Jelly Lord Paul liked it very well so Jelly Roll asked to come to the rehearsal and that they could go over this tune which he did and he had another tune called London Blues and that particular time Paul and Rap were going to record Millen Boy Joys they never had any first part to it voice and Jelly Roll put the first part to the Millen Boy Joys and they gave him part of it

yeah Paul went to McDonough 9 and then Aloysius and that's the fire of the sea

none at all my dad didn't even want to fool with the trumpet because the neighbors used to squawk and everything else because he was blasting out there but Paul had it and Paul was real good Paul never got real just that he should have he Paul was a real fine trumpet man real New Orleans played the lead and could swing a band and really could rock a band and Paul really made a good band
I heard him play one night up there when he had the barbecue on Monday nights seems that everybody has these sessions Monday nights on his barbecue place up on State Street did you ever see that

oh yeah I was there in fact in 36 I believe it was I was up there when Paul used to have he had the P&M then at that time that's the one where I went well he had all the jam sessions of course the Bobcats were there Eddie Miller Bob Zerkey and he used to have Baby Dodds because Baby Dodds was his favorite drummer and he used to send for Lee Collins all the time and Warren Smith and Georgie and all of them all the top jazz men in that territory around Chicago would always come out to Paul's and they'd all jam and have some of them real real good old New Orleans jam sessions Paul never gave it up he always liked it and Paul was a good jazz man that is from all around from trying to keep it going and playing it and what you call sleeping it eating it and everything else Paul was a real jazz man all the way around Bill he loved it and he's never knocked anybody he's always tried to help and tried to do the right thing

he was a very wonderful fellow I only knew him a couple of nights you might say we were working on the book Jazzman I went there to interview him in 1938 I remember one Monday session maybe more than one at that time he didn't seem to be playing regularly I mean he had this little restaurant so he must have given up music professionally
he wouldn't hold a lip and like I say he'd have Lee Collins there and Mac Portland you know when
his last regular job was though

yeah in 1934 at Harry's New York Ball that was his last band in fact right about a year before Paul died he came down to New Orleans the owner of the Blue Note gave Paul permission to come pick up a band and he came down to New Orleans and I even went around with him and he had Santo on trombone he had Fasola on clarinet he had Lester Boucher on tenor and himself would be on trumpet and he had George Wetland on drums that he had left in Chicago and Jess Stacy and Pat Patterson that was the band that Paul wanted to put together but when he went back to Chicago Paul wasn't feeling too well he was sick at that time he didn't know it and Paul just went on and on and that's it What was about
the exact date did you give the date of his death about?
Well he died on August 18th 1949 49
Can you think of anything else about him did he play in a school band
or anything else

I don't think they had too many school bands they couldn't even buy instruments Where did he get
his first horn anything about that?
It was my daddy's I said yeah my daddy played the trumpet and he picked it up and practiced on it and played on it that's the way you got it
Yeah

But Bill just like I say I never gave up on jazz I'm going to continue with my little Southland label and it's dedicated to all the New Orleans jazz men I have as I say I have all the greats on it and anyone or any bands that I see fit that I think will sound New Orleans I'm going to record them and I'm going to keep this going I have good recordings on Papa Celestine I made the last recording that the old gent made before he passed away I made the last one at Tom Brown I thought I want to ask
some more about Tom Brown when was the first time anything that you can think of about Tom Brown Well I didn't

know Tom too well I mean in the early years but I got to know Tom later on in life and in fact in the last ten years before he died Tom and I got to be very very good friends and those are the kind of things maybe we can bring that little point out that hurt I'm going to give you two men what I mean is this let's take Johnny St. Cyr for instance there's a fella who was the name of the Louis Armstrong band in the 25s a fella that was truly one of the real greats and he comes on all these years and nobody took time out to give the fella a band the front foot that he could say I had a little band myself well I feel very proud that I finally gave Johnny St. Cyr that chance and I fronted him with a terrific band and it came out real good and I'm happy for Johnny because Johnny is a real great fella all the way around I can say that now getting back to Tom Tom's in the history of jazz Tom gets credit for bringing the first white band up there Tom's done lots of good for jazz has done it all the time and I'm surprised that nobody's took time out again to give the old gent something for himself that he can remember and his people can remember and I'm proud again that I had the thought to take Tom and put him in front of a band of his own of a lot of the greats here in New Orleans surrounding with the greats and we came had another good session and Tom was very happy of it because Tom never wanted to record unless he had what he wanted what it sounded like it had to be what Tom Brown liked and when I played him back he says this is exactly what I want and I was happy for it and three weeks later Tom passed away so that's about all I can tell you now Bill

no no my brother Rene my brother Vic's at the post office but Rene and I yeah Rene and I in these raw foyer business and alligator I never know his

oh yes my daddy was in the business and we carried it on from my daddy
where was he located

he went well he was located here in the 500 block of Decatur and later in the 20s he went on Chapitulas and South Peterson Gravia and Paul worked also the foyer business in those years nearly after he came back from when he gave up music in the 23 24 when the Rhythm Kings broke up and rap got sick and Georgie Brunas went with Ted Lewis Paul came on home and he worked the fur business
then he

anything else about your fur business not that that has too much to do with the music
but most of the fellas at times I know worked at other jobs. Did Paul start in any other job down here? He was so young before he left home. Did he work at anything then?

Yes, in 1930 he opened a Chicago barbecue here on Magnolia and Washington. And he ran that a few years because I remember Louie visiting there, him and Louie eating all them barbecues. Can we talk about Louie? We mean Louie Armstrong. And any of the musicians that came down visiting, and now you take later on when Paul Whiteman played here. Paul, we all lived out in Metry Ridge then. We had three homes. That was in the early 30s then. And Bix and some in Frankie Trembar, and those boys all came out to Paul's and Monk and Armand Hug and...
When did he go back to Chicago then?
Well, he went back to Chicago, I think, around in 30... 32. In 1934 he went to Harry's New York Ball with the band.
That's a similar band they had recorded for, the OK that time.
Well, that is the band.
It was Omer Simeon wasn't with him though, was he?
Omer Simeon took Fazola's place. They were waiting. You see, Hobie Carmichael got the date for Paul.
I heard that.

Yes, he got the date for Paul to record four sides. And Fazola was supposed to play with Paul's outfit and he just couldn't make it. And the date was scheduled for that day and they used Omer Simeon at that time.
Simeon never worked at Harry's Bar then.
No, no, no, no. Santo, Pecora, Paul and Boyce Brown was the front line. You remember Boyce? Yeah. He played alto. And of course, Jess Stacy and Pat Patterson.
We were talking about the OK date then. Harry's New Yorker.

Well, I mentioned Jess Stacy was on piano. In fact, Paul recommended Jess Stacy to Benny Goodman. And that's where Jess went into Ben Goodman for Paul's recommendation. Of course, Benny Goodman is very good friends with Paul. In fact, Benny played for Paul's wedding when he was in short pants. Really? Yeah, Benny was only at that time 16 years old.
I met Paul's wife. She was the brother of some police captain or something? Yeah, her brother Tom was captain of police
in the first district of Chicago.
Chicago district.
That's right. She had two brothers also that were sergeants and was a big police family.
Yeah, I remember. What was their name again?

Harrison's. Tommy Harrison and her name was Marie Harrison. But at that time, Paul had an awful good band and they sort of brought back jazz in that 34 because at that time they were the only band playing what they felt like playing. They weren't told to play this, tell them to play that, just Paul kicked the tunes off and they played what they wanted. And I spoke to a lot of musicians at that time and they all said that this band was probably swinging a jazz band, Dixieland band in the nation at that time because they all used to come watch it. I mean, Earl Heinz, Duke Ellington, all that stood in the kitchen and listened to the band. They all liked it. Bill, do you want to get back to the little label? Southway?

Yes, there's other things you can tell. As I say, 50 years when we're all gone, people are going to have all sorts of rumors about these records and the studio and everything else here. We might mention a little bit more about the studio. It's in a back room here. Did you build this especially? It's back away from the street where it's entirely soundproof.
Well, I did build a room, yes, in the back of the office and we have it soundproof and that's where we had a good set of drums, a bass and a good upright piano.
Air-conditioned too, I might say.
Air-conditioned and we have all the collector's items in the record department here, practically all 78s. I got all the Jeanette's and the King Oliver's and the Louis Armstrong's.
Most of your personal collection is here then, is it?

Well, a great deal of it, but some of the real collector's things I have away, make sure they don't get broken and so forth. And we have some old instruments, as you can see, trombone, clarinet, old trumpets here. We've got an old bass tuba that Chink Martin played on lots of times. And I've got, in the background here, I've got Monk Hazel's mellophone.

Oh, yeah. And we always got... I was going to say, does anybody ever kid you? I notice in your, it looks like you're lined up here for a session almost with a lot of chairs, including two rocking chairs. Does anybody kid you about using some of the old-timers that can't walk anymore have to sit in a rocking chair? Well, I haven't got to that yet. Not yet. Not yet. Very comfortable-looking studio. I was laughing about those rocking chairs on myself. And actually, some of these old-timers have more pep than the young kids, if you ask me. If we don't mind going over some of these sessions, you can tell which ones were done here in this studio. Some of the things you've issued have been done right here.

Well, I did the Sharky with these Kings of Dixieland, and I call it the Sharky and the Jam Session in New Orleans here. That's my 205, and I made it right here in the studio. We have some live applause there, which naturally I added to it. And I've done the Monk Hazel Session in here. That's the 217. Those are the only two that I've really done in this studio.

Where were most of them done, if you don't mind telling? Well, at different spots, Bill. Any trade secrets? No, no, there's no trade, too. I mean, you know what I mean. It would be interesting for people someday to know, because on the label it doesn't tell exactly, and nobody usually tells, and they won't know unless someone like you will tell them.

Well, my 207 and Mardi Gras Parade music from New Orleans, we have things like King Zulu, and I'll Cease to Love and those tunes, and we made that at the Woodman and Royal Hall. It's a big open hall, and naturally we had to get the outside effect, and sort of an echoes outside, and we used the big hall for that. I've done probably eight or ten of them at WDSU here in New Orleans. I've used, lately I've used Dan's Pierce 600 at 501 Boybman Street, where Al Hoyt appears nightly. The acoustics are very, very fine there, and the recordings come out real good. In different spots, I used one of them at the Legion Hall, out on Canal Boulevard when I had it, and probably when I first started in 54, I made the Johnny Wiggs session there.
At the Legion Hall. I thought maybe it was at Lentz or something. No, no, it was across the street from Lentz.
They called it, they had two or three different names. Anyhow, I called it the Legion Hall. And we made that and they have the Johnny Wiggs, which got some real, real good reviews,
especially for Harry Shields and Tom Brown was on that one,
and he got some great reviews, and Johnny Wiggs.
Was it a place where there was music there?

Yes, the Basin Street Six was playing there at that time, and I got the job for Johnny Wiggs and his outfit, and I came over one night and I says, Johnny, I'm going to do a little recording this band. I like it, it sounds good, it's got the old-time sound. In fact, that session put me in the business. I tried to sell it to two or three of the smaller record companies, nobody didn't like it, and I thought, well, something's wrong here. I'm going to have to try this thing myself. I did, and I sent it to a record changer in different spots and downbeat and all, and they thought it was terrific, so that put me in business. I thought I'd go on and make some more of them, which I did. I made the George Girard and the Jack Delaney and the George Lewis. By the way, I recorded George Lewis in the studio. That's something that George didn't have much chance to do.
The radio like WDSU, you mean?
Ah, yes, I recorded George at WDSU, and I got a real nice recording of George, and like I said, done in the studio, and we took time out to tune up.
Yeah.
And different sessions I made, that's about the biggest spots. I made some of them at WTPS, which had a fine studio also.
Got the old Howard Memorial library.
Right, and I also made a few. For instance, I think the Jack Delaney, I made at WSMB. So I kicked around here where I thought the sound was best for that particular band.

One question I was going to ask, maybe doesn't belong on here, but Jack Delaney's father, of course, is a taxi driver. Every once in a while, I get in his cab, and was he ever a musician? Would he be a good one? Yes, he did.
He played alto sax.
Would he be a good one for an interview, you think, for him?
Well, I don't know if he's... Let me...
Okay, we were talking about Jack Delaney's father.

Well, Jack's father just drives a cab just two or three hours a day, mostly to get out the house. He's a retired fireman on pension today. He played a little alto sax in the days where he used to play for the house parties. You know, when he had the little alto sax and C melody, and he never really got to play any jazz or anything like that. Of course, he's got a fine boy there that plays a lot of trombone, Jack. Jack's terrific. He has the makings. I think Jack will be in years to come if he sticks to the Dixieland.
Well, he's working at the hotel there the last few years.

He's up to with that now. Yeah, he took it away from him a little, but he's getting back into the Dixieland vein now, and he'll probably come back. He's playing around now with Sharky and some of the real Dixieland boys, so it'll bring back Jack to the field that he belongs in. Anything else, Bill?
I was going to ask some more about some of those sessions, the Celestan session. Do you mind telling us where that was, or do you remember anything about the details of that?

That's how I'm glad you brought that up. Papa Celesty and I were very, very good friends. I like the old man. The old man is very kind. He's very generous, and he's well-liked by everybody. If he needed anybody for benefits, anything, he was right there willing. I went over, after I started my little label, I went up to his house one Sunday afternoon. I says, Papa, you know something? I got everybody who's who in New Orleans but you. I got to have you on my label. He says, son, he says, with a little smile, he says, I believe you're just a little bit too late. He said, the Columbia people were here yesterday, and I haven't signed yet, but he said, I think I might make a deal with them. So he says, what do you have to offer? I says, well, you know, I'm just a little small label here in New Orleans, just trying to keep jazz alive. Most I can offer you is the scale for side. So he kind of smiled, and he says, well, you know me. He says, I'm part of New Orleans just like you. He said, I'm going to record for your label on scale, but he said, son, I can get triple that from Columbia, but he said, I think I'm going to go along with you. I made the session with Papa, and we went up to WDSU. The tunes that requested most by Papa are tunes like Marie Laveau, Down by the Riverside, The Saints, Didn't He Ramble, so I thought I would put these on. And we went to WDSU and recorded, and I remember the last tune we played. This is the last time Papa recorded, and we played Down by the Riverside, and he sang it, and he played a little solo at the end, which I crossed my fingers. I didn't really think he'd make the high note, and he did. I turned around to Papa, and I said to him, How did this feel to you? And the old gent had tears in his eyes, and he said, This tune moved me more than of any tune I can remember, and that's Down by the Riverside, and that's the last tune the old gent ever played. And I always thought it was real nice that he came on my label, which was a very good thing, because Papa's a very, very live man to be on any recording label, because everybody wants him.
It's surprising, even ten years, well, not ten years, it was six years since he died, and that's right,

and he still wanted, and everybody was loyal to Papa. In the old days when everybody was going out of town, Papa stayed around, and he got to play for a lot of the boys that's coming up now as fathers and mothers for their weddings and parties and everything, and everybody remembers old Papa Celestine, so any time Papa's playing any spot in New Orleans, it might be the country club or here, they'll say, Go here, Papa Celestine, he played for your mama's wedding, or this and so forth. So the old man was liked by everybody, he was a real great fellow.
The Tom Brown session, where was that done?
We did the Tom Brown session at WDSU also.
You usually had rehearsals over here though.

Yeah, we always put the session together here, we map out and we get our patterns here, who's going to play this and what's what, and go over the tunes, and exchange a few ideas. I have my own ideas what I want, but I always like to hear things and suggestions, and we always put them together and see, and as a rule, they always come out real nice. And Tom, like I said, we spoke a little further back on the tape, that Tom was very, very, I don't know exactly how to put it, but he wanted things right.
Yeah.

And he said he'd never record unless he got exactly what he wanted, and that's exactly what happened on the session I gave him. Like I told you earlier in the tape, when we played the tapes back, I says, Tom, what do you think of me? He says, exactly what I wanted.
I remember, I'm not trying to give any secrets right, but I think Eden had one of the agreements is the publicity and what went on, all the companies and everything. Oh yeah, he wanted,
he gave me a list of things that he wanted done.
I heard about that.

But after we got talking and sat on and I pointed out to him this and thing, he told me, he said, you're right, Joe, I had a little heart on this thing and go ahead and do it the way you think it should be done. I'll leave it all in your hands and after that, we agreed that it was the right thing to do. And he was very satisfied and he tore up the papers of the little rules that he wanted. But I'll tell you why. Tom had done a little recording before and he wasn't satisfied. He was a side man but it seems like a couple of things that he did, I mean, the band wasn't up to par
and they weren't

at their best and they came out anyhow and Tom didn't like it which I don't blame Tom. When you're going to record, that's on there for keeps and for years to come and if you don't do it right, they'll say, well, who was Tom Brown? Listen to this. he couldn't play anything and so forth and all. But anyhow, I'm happy to say that he was very satisfied in my session and I was glad that I could give another good old fella a band of his own.
Yeah, he doesn't seem really old to me. he's been
around for ages, but he died so suddenly I didn't even know it. He'd been sick. He wasn't sick when he, what was it, pneumonia that he took? Well, he took pneumonia, but he had

a collapsed lung. In fact, the last tune I made on a session, I had to cut his solo out because he couldn't make it. Was that something in recent years or later? I don't know. I didn't know it, but I understand he played with one lung. Actually, he looked so small
he didn't look so healthy, but yet those small people like that sometimes. That's right.
He could go. He went on and went on. I like Tom. Tom was good people. He didn't have a
cold or pneumonia. No, but he went into pneumonia. Right after that. That was it. Are there any more of those sessions that you want to go through? Any other things about?

Well, there's two or three other boys here. For instance, we take like Joe Capera. Back in the early 30s, Joe was one of the big names around New Orleans. In fact, he was the only one who had a band around here. Joe faded out. I brought Joe back also after 20 years' retirement. In my book, Joe's one of the greatest guitar boys in the business. He's a good rhythm boy. He knows what it's all about. Another fellow here I'd like to bring on is Charlie Cadela. Charlie and my brother Paul were very, very good friends. I've always been good friends with Charlie all my life. I always enjoyed his playing. I thought Charlie was one of the greats that belong up there with Sidney Arrigan and Raymond Boyk and rap and Fars and those kind of fellas. And I did want to have Charlie on my label. Well, Charlie had been retired for about 20 years also. So I said, look, man, start fooling with that clarinet in about a month from now, I'm going to come back at you. I don't want no finance. I'm telling you to start playing a little bit. Well, about a month I came back. He said, well, I believe I can make four tunes. I said, well, here, I got four tunes picked. How do they sound to you? Well, he said, three of them's all right. Give me nobody, sweetheart, because I like that tune and I know it. I said, well, it's yours. So we made the session and that came out very good. And you still can hear Charlie with that beautiful harmonizing clarinet that was so popular in the early days. Sounded a lot like the rap's tone sometimes. You can hardly tell them apart. And he's still got that real harmony parts there that really made a good feeling in the band. Another man, Zemiel Christian, who'd been around and he
never gave up music, but nobody knew he was alive hardly playing bass. I'm glad you brought
him up too, because he's another fella that finally got to front his own band. You know,
I'm confused on this record myself. I've never listened to it so much as I should have, but I know there are two trombones on it. Can you remember which tunes Emil plays any solo? Oh,

yeah. Well, of course, in the later years, Emil went to bass. He gave up the trombone. But when I give this session to Emil, I had to have him on some trombone parts. So I got a good band back, Emil. I got Mike Lala, good trumpet man here, good lead trumpet man, and Harry Shields on clarinet, and Bob Havens, who's one of the real fine trombone players here around New Orleans today. Of course, Joe Cupero on banjo and Monk Hazel on drums, Armand Hug on piano. And I thought I would record a few tunes, and one or two of them I'd use two trombones. And this I did. Of course, naturally, I have a little tune I wrote called A Mardi Gras Parade. And we need a lot of tailgate, we need a lot of trombone. And I use Emil all the way through on trombone along with Bob Havens. And then we go on to a little tune called Lost My Heart in Dixieland, which was recorded by the original Dixieland band. Of course, Emil was a member of that band. And I used two trombones. And let me bring this out too, Bill. On this particular session, I used Harry Shields, but I bought Raymond Boykin. They also played two clarinets on two of the tunes. I think it, you always hurt the one you love. And also, I lost my heart in Dixieland. And of course, Raymond and Harry make a wonderful team together. And that came out marvelous. In fact, it's the reviewers give this four stars where anyone that reviews it, they think it's one of the finest things I've done.
So Christian only plays trombone on a couple of the numbers.

That's all. He plays on the Mardi Gras Parade all the way through. And then on the Lost My Heart in Dixieland, he takes a solo with Bob Havens. They take a two trombone solo. So Emil Christians is another one that I've had the good faith of and happy to say that I gave him a band also, that this old gent could also say that he had a band of his own for his family or from years to come, you know, that he had something to a band of his own.
Another fellow who's gone now, young Abby Brunis, the drummer. Do you have any recollections of him?

Oh, very much so. He was also a very good friend of mine. And I know Abby, we came up together. And Abby was a real fine Dixieland drummer too. In fact, I put him with Sharky when he started to come back playing Dixieland. That was in 1952. And he stayed with Sharky until he died. But Abby was a good boy. He's the nephew of the Merritt and Abby Brunis and Henry and the real Brunis family, Georgie and them. And the boy was just about hitting his height when he went on to Beyond's.
I understand that you helped Lizzie Miles with her comeback too.

Yes, I did, Bill. Well, Lizzie had been retired about 13 years. And she was working a little spot, wasn't doing too good. And Lizzie was dying to make a comeback. She rode a couple of disc jockeys here, didn't pay any attention to her. Well, I had a little radio program of my own for four and a half years, plugging Dixieland at WSMB. And I also took a little time on Tony Almerickas. Tony at that time was ill. So I went on for him for two weeks. In the meantime, I had the Johnny Saint-Cien, Paul Barber, George Lewis, and all the big names as guests. So one Friday afternoon, I got in touch with Lizzie and I asked her to come on up. I want to interview her on the air. I brought her up there and I said, Lizzie, how's your voice? She says, well, after 13 years, she said, I think it's more powerful today than it was in the early 20s. So I said, well, all right, I'm going to try you out Sunday evening. So I brought her to a concert and let Lizzie sing a couple of tunes. She brought the house down. So I walked over that evening and I, to a friend of mine, Steve Villani, who has the Paddock Club on Boydman Street, and I said, Steve, put Lizzie Miles to work. I must say so. And that's, she came back. I made a record date with her on my Southland. I got her a capital contract and I brought Lizzie into Linfen's Lounge to play the concerts with Shockey and so forth. And I think I've done a little bit to help Lizzie. Yeah, I'm sure. I've heard of that before. And while we're talking about helping some different musicians, I was very, very glad to help little Pete Fountain. Pete wasn't doing too much around here. And then in 1956, I engineered a job out on the West Coast with Frank Bull and Gene Norman, where they hold the Dixieland
Jubilee. I was going to ask about those trips that you made out there too.

Well, I brought Al Hoyt and I brought little Warren Luling and Pete Fountain. And I engineered that job because they never had Hoyt any other boys that I brought out there. And I told Pete at that time, I said, Pete, you're playing a lot of clarinet and maybe if the right people would hear you, maybe you'd get a break. And it's exactly what happened. Lawrence Welk's boy happened to be in the audience. He told his daddy he heard a terrific clarinet player. We gave Pete his tunes, Tin Roof Blues and the March of the Bobcats and the Jazz Me Blues, which he, was his crib numbers, which he does very, very good. We put a sub mic up there and Pete knocked him out. Well, the rest is history with Pete. He finally went with Lawrence Welk. And today Pete's a big name.
What was the first year you went out there?

Well, in 1954, Frank Bullas wrote down here in New Orleans and asked me to get a bunch together. And I brought Raymond Boyk, Jack Delaney, Johnny St. Cyr and little Georgie Girard. And we competed that year with eight bands and we came out on top.
That's on the record, by the way. The Gene Norman Presents record is still available.

It's still available. But we really laid him in the aisle and it gave those boys a nice break. It gave Georgie Girard a good break. And like I say, George could have went on to big and better things if Miss Fortune wouldn't have took him and passed away. But I get a kick out of trying to help a few of the boys. If I can do anything to give them just a little bit of help. Like I said, Bill, Dixieland's in my heart. I love it. I guess I always will. And I like the music and I like the boys. And if I can help them anyway and I'll keep on plugging. I'll keep on making Southlands. And like I say, you never know who's going to hear you. And some of them might get a break out of it. There's quite a few boys like little Dutch Andrews and them that got their first recording date with me. I recorded quite a bit of the names. Tony Peretti and Georgie Brunas. I finally got Georgie on my label. And I have quite a few of the real boys.

I was going to ask, do you know of anyone else we could interview about the New Orleans Rhythm Kings? Are there any other of your relatives, family that could tell us anything about Paul's history? Any better than not that I'm, I don't mean that. Well, I don't think so. I mean, anybody would have other angles on him or anything, you know, that would knew him? No, I took, I took

to the jazz. You were the nearest teenage to him. That's right. I stayed with it. No, my brother Rene is right back. He's right back. Oh, yeah. But he know any other more details of him? No, he wouldn't know because he didn't follow that. He didn't have the interest in the music. That's right. He didn't follow like I did. I liked it. I wanted to play it. And I got a big kick out of it. And wherever jazz was played, you could see me sitting there. All concerts at any place that had any jazz at all, I would be there listening. Do you think there are any of
Rapp's folks, some sisters living, would they have any interest that we could interview them, do you think, about Rapp? You could, but I don't think they could tell you

too much about Rapp. They didn't follow Rapp's life too much, you see. I don't think they could really help you on anything in Rapp. They had one boy, he passed away, a little Georgie, a little Gerard boy here. He used to play alto sax. He followed the Rhythm Kings, went up there with him. Si Gerard is his name. When he passed away two years ago, he could tell you a lot about Rapp, Paul and Georgie and a lot of nice things about it. I'd like to, as I
say, you're the only one I can think of that really would know much about Paul. Can you tell us anything else about this style of playing? Did he ever use mutes that you know much?

Oh yeah. Well, Paul always followed the Oliver tradition. He liked King Oliver. I know he told me that himself. Yeah, yeah, that was his idol. I talked to him. King Oliver, at least, was Paul's idol. And if you recall, Bill, King Oliver was a real mute man himself. I didn't know that Paul ever used mutes. Oh yeah, Paul, oh yeah, you can get the early Jeanettes and you can see he has that mute effect like King Oliver. I didn't remember much of that. Oh yeah, oh yeah, very, very, Paul used the mute all the time. Yeah, plenty of times. He followed the Oliver, he liked Oliver and in fact he tried to copy Oliver. That was a big job. Ain't nobody could do it, but he tried. He had a peculiar style. Yeah, he had his own style which was one of the tops too.

Can you think, did he ever tell you anything or you of course have done more work probably on research in the New Orleans Rhythm Kings than anyone I know, any details about those sessions that isn't, a lot of that's been written up. Anything that isn't widely known about those sessions? I mean, they were all in Richmond, Indiana, I guess, weren't they? Yeah, that's right. They went over there. Anything about the trips over there that you can remember?

Well, it's a funny thing, Bill, about those things. I spoke to Steve Brown, who made some of those sessions. I talked with Mel Stetzel, who made a lot of them, Georgie Brunas. None of them remember anything vivid. Well, you don't get much detail. No, you can't get details. In fact, Georgie Brunas can't tell you who was on the session. Believe it or not, he can't. If you said, Georgie, who was on this particular tune and so forth, he saw this guy and that guy and he's got them all wrong. Sometimes the piano player changed around a lot. Yeah, they had Kyle and they had Jell-A-Roll, Martin, they had Mel Stetzel, they had Elvis Schoenberg, four or five different piano players played on different records. But they don't remember and I don't know, you get back to those old time musicians and all, you just can't get the thing straightened out. And these jazz books they put out, they all...
And it really gets mixed up. I just thought maybe you might remember certain things that maybe you heard from Paul or other people that you've talked to about these sessions that isn't widely known.

And these jazz book fellows that do this writing for these jazz books, they'll come down here and always contact the wrong people. And if they do, they're going to get the wrong information. And if they run into a certain group, they'll tell them they did everything. They wrote jazz, they made jazz and they did it all, you see. And they really don't get the right story of these things. But I hope it keeps going, Bill.
Anything about any of those tunes on the Jeanette, the Angry, that's the Brunus Brothers.
Well, that's the Brunus Boys, yeah, that's their tune. And of course, the Tin Roof Blues was Paul and Rap and George's and finally they split it with the band.
We've mentioned the Millenberg and the...

Millenberg and the... Now the Farewell Blues was made right on the bandstand. After Paul told me, of course, they used to play from seven to seven, you know, in those days, when they played at the Fryers Inn. And all the boys used to come listen to them. Bix was one of the... Every night is there, till they almost had to throw him out the joint. Bix and Benny Goodman and Mac Port.

And all that Austin High Gang, Teshmark and the whole bunch tried to come in and listen to the New Orleans Rhythm Kings. Now, getting back to the Farewell Blues, after a session one time, Rap was looking for some harmonies with Paul, and they ran into the Farewell Blues, and they called it the Railroad Blues, because they had those wah-wah effects, you know, and they called it Railroad Blues, and finally called it the Farewell Blues.

I know when I first met George Brunus, 1936 in New York, I gave him a couple of those Jeanette records, and he said that Farewell Blues is something that Rap worked that out of the weary blues. He took a little phrase out of the weary blues.

Well, it has that Shake It and Break It deal in there. And a lot of them record a lot of their own tunes, the Bugle called Rag and things like that. They were made up, and they lost a lot of tunes. For instance, Alma Schobert was the only fellow could read in the band, and what I hear, he copied a lot of things that later on he used, like Nobody's Sweetheart, Copenhagen, and I know for a fact that Paul wrote the tune called, I Never Knew What A Gal Could Do. Alma Schobert gets credit for it, but I'm sure Paul wrote this tune, which I hear.
They're going to hear OK.

Well, they call it Zero, and today they call it Zero, but the real name I was, I Never Knew What A Gal Could Do. Alma Schobert gets credit. You were just smart enough to take the thing, and that's all right.
I was going to ask about the Victor session, too. Do you remember any details of that?

Yes, I do. That Victor session, Victor people came out here and contacted Paul, and they liked the band. That was the 1925 band. It was here in New Orleans. Well, Paul had a lot of, I don't want to say a lot, but he had bad luck in it. Charlie Cudelo was going to play tenor sax, Santa and trombone, and Red Long and Leo Addy, and that particular day they were going to record, Santo and Rap had a little falling out. So Rap walked off the set, and Paul went through it anyhow, and he made Charlie get off the tenor and go on to clarinet, Charlie Cudelo. That's how that happened. Yeah, and he took the Crying For Me blues solo, but he wouldn't take it like Rap took it, so he changed it around and so forth and so on, but that's what happened on that particular session. They just had to have a little hard feelings that day when they were going to record, and Rap walked off.
The O.K.'s were made down here too, weren't they?
That's right.
That was before or after the Victor, do you think?
That was before.
I think that those dates are known, I believe.
No, I remember that very well, the O.K. recording time, because they rehearsed on Broad and Espanade in my home.
Oh, they did.

Oh, yeah, they rehearsed the tunes, and they call it the Golden Leaf Stretch, which is the Millen Boy can see, and in those days, Bill, I guess you know it, the boys used to smoke the marijuana, and it used to be wrapped in the yellow paper, so they called it the Golden Leaf Strut. And then they recorded the She's Crying For Me blues, which Santo put together, Santo Picor, and they also never knew what a gal could do, and I forget the other tune. Yeah, some pop-sounding tune.

Sounds like a late pop tune almost. Well, I think that about covers everything. Maybe later, if we think of some more things, another day we can come and talk another half hour if you think of everything. All right, Bill. I certainly appreciate you taking time off from your business.
Well, it was a pleasure, and I just hope jazz can continue, and fellas like you and some of the other boys around here are really doing a good job at it. Thank you.
